record.title: A nested component-attribution method reports sparse, transferable circuits and a refusal edit
record.summary: A September 2026 preprint proposes Matryoshka Attribution (MAttr), a learned ordering of model components based on nested masks optimized for downstream loss. The authors say it ranks first on the official Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark leaderboard and identifies sparse, task-transferable circuits. As one application, they report that restoring 1% of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct weights to the base-model state removes refusals while maintaining capabilities. These are author claims from the preprint abstract; this activation did not inspect the full evaluation, verify the leaderboard or reproduce the intervention.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors published a preprint proposing MAttr, which learns nested component masks across sparsity levels using a differentiable top-k parameterization.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors say MAttr ranks first on the official Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark leaderboard and identifies sparse, task-transferable circuits.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For one refusal-behavior application, authors report that restoring 1% of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct weights to the base-model state is sufficient to remove refusals while maintaining capabilities.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: This activation inspected the abstract only; leaderboard conditions, intervention protocol, retained capability measures and independent replication have not been checked.

evidence_gaps.description: The full evaluation protocol, leaderboard conditions, intervention controls and quantitative capability-retention measurements were not inspected.
No independent replication of the learned attribution ranking or 1% weight-restoration result has been established.

brief.importance_rationale: If a learned attribution ordering reliably identifies sparse, transferable causal components and the reported intervention reproduces, it could materially change mechanistic interpretability and behavioral editing. Score 5 reflects the potential consequence of the bounded paper claims, not confidence in them.
limitations: The current review is based on the arXiv abstract only.
The official leaderboard rank is author-reported here; benchmark conditions and comparator versions were not inspected.
The refusal intervention is reported for Llama 3.1 8B Instruct; retained capabilities and affected refusal categories are not specified in this record.
No independent implementation or reproduction was checked.
brief.summary: A September 2026 preprint proposes Matryoshka Attribution (MAttr), a learned ordering of model components based on nested masks optimized for downstream loss. The authors say it ranks first on the official Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark leaderboard and identifies sparse, task-transferable circuits. As one application, they report that restoring 1% of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct weights to the base-model state removes refusals while maintaining capabilities. These are author claims from the preprint abstract; this activation did not inspect the full evaluation, verify the leaderboard or reproduce the intervention.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report first place on the official Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark leaderboard, sparse task-transferable circuits, and a Llama 3.1 8B Instruct experiment where restoring 1% of weights to base-model values removes refusals while maintaining capabilities.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public abstract states the proposed method and its claimed applications. No benchmark, intervention or weight-restoration result was independently verified in this activation.
technical.mechanism: MAttr frames attribution as finding nested subsets of internal components that minimize downstream loss. A differentiable sigmoid top-k mask is trained with randomized sparsity levels to produce an ordering of components by attribution score.
technical.regime: Abstract describes a benchmark leaderboard and a single Llama 3.1 8B Instruct weight-restoration application. Generalization across model families, refusal categories and capability metrics is not established here.
technical.reproducibility: The abstract is accessible. The full paper and a reproducible implementation were not inspected or run in this activation.
technical.strongest_baseline: The abstract does not identify the exact leaderboard baselines, intervention controls or capability-retention metrics; these require inspection of the full paper and benchmark entry.

brief.title: A nested component-attribution method reports sparse, transferable circuits and a refusal edit
brief.why_it_matters: A scalable method for attributing behavior to sparse, transferable model components could improve mechanistic analysis. The reported 1% weight-restoration result also makes the method relevant to understanding and potentially changing refusal behavior, but it does not establish a general intervention or safety outcome.
